video.title: Psychology of Charisma: How To Actually Make People Like You

protocol.status: pilot -- one draft labeler (Claude agent) plus one human reviewer, not issue 011's two independent labelers
protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output.
protocol.times_from: Whisper small transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Cold open: charisma advice aims at the wrong target; charisma isn't something people see in you, it's how they feel about themselves around you. Ends before 'Welcome back to PsychToons'.
The 2018 Toronto study split charisma into influence and affability; all popular advice trains influence, which reads as intensity, not charisma.

Reis and Shaver's perceived partner responsiveness: understanding, validation, caring; nothing on the list is about you. 'You do not generate liking, you create the conditions.' Can open on the question 'what is affability made of?' at 144.6.
Fiske's warmth vs competence: warmth is judged first because 'are you going to hurt me?' came before 'how skilled are you?'. Ends on heat vs light: brilliant but cold to stand next to.

'It's not stupidity, it's training': school, interviews, social media all grade performance, so we audition. Two good ends: 317.5 ('nobody makes money telling you to think about yourself less') or 350.9 ('you're not failing because you're boring, you're failing because you're busy'). The range is wide on purpose.
Boothby 2018 liking-gap study: people systematically underestimate how much they are liked because they grade their own performance, and the trap that follows.
'Just be confident' fails: confidence is an output, not an input. Antonakis trained managers in charismatic behaviors and blind raters scored them higher: same people, different moves.
Law 1: follow-up questions drive liking (Harvard speed-dating data); 'that is two people taking turns waiting'. Self-contained, with an actionable ending.

Law 3: people underestimate how good a compliment feels (Zhao and Epley); 'nice shirt is noise', a specific compliment proves you paid attention. Whisper merged its end with 'Law four' (the cut is at ~636.7).
Law 4: capitalization, where how you respond to good news predicts closeness; don't deflate it, ask for the story. 'People remember exactly who let them be happy out loud.'
Law 5: the beautiful mess effect. Our own vulnerability looks like weakness to us and courage to others; one honest sentence is enough.
Law 6: Moreland and Beach 1992, where women who silently attended more lectures were rated warmer. Liking is built by frequency, not one brilliant encounter.

negatives.why: Channel intro promising 'six laws that make people genuinely like you, all backed by real research'. A strong hook with no payoff inside the cut.
Closing reflection with the Simone Weil 'attention is the rarest form of generosity' quote. It is quotable, but it opens on 'practice these six' and leans on the whole video.
Comment prompt listing the six laws, then 'remember what the liking gap tells us: people already like you more than you think'. A strong line, but it is a callback inside the outro.
Like / share-with-a-friend / subscribe call to action.

also_ok.why: Law 2: lead with warmth, not credentials. Competence introduced first is judged, after warmth it is admired. 'Remember what Fiske found' is a light callback, but the next sentence restates the finding, so it holds up. Starting at 541.8 skips the callback but loses the law's title.

Short version of the payoff in 'trained-to-audition': the harder you try to be liked the worse you get, because attention on yourself is attention not on them. 'You're failing because you are busy.' About 28s.
Shorter cut of 'confidence-is-an-output': charisma is behavior and behavior can be installed; Antonakis's trained managers were rated more charismatic by blind raters. About 34s.
